risk_long: Mechanics could log codes for tyres riders did not actually buy, or collude with retailers to fabricate recommendations.
control_long: One credit per tyre serial; a monthly cap per member; random IVR call-backs to riders named on the sale; a distance flag between retailer and mechanic beyond A21 km; distributor audit of the top earners each quarter.

risk_long: The retailer has no strong incentive to take the extra step of entering the mechanic code at the point of sale, so the loop breaks at step 3.
control_long: The retailer earns a small logging credit inside its own existing loyalty scheme for every code entered, giving it a reason to log; the programme is piloted with retailer training before scale.

risk_long: Initial sign-up enthusiasm fades once the starter kit is in hand and no further engagement follows.
control_long: Quarterly consumable refills create a recurring reason to log codes; the six-month tier review risks loss of status and tools, which behavioural evidence shows is a stronger motivator than a one-off gift; WhatsApp tips keep the programme visible between refills.

risk_long: Distributors who are asked to enrol mechanics may deprioritise it against their core stocking and selling work.
control_long: A per-enrolment incentive (A17) paid to distributor sales staff; a missed-call or WhatsApp self-enrolment path that does not depend on a distributor visit; monthly enrolment targets reviewed with distributors.

risk_long: A competitor could launch a similar tools-and-status programme once ours is visible in the market.
control_long: The stock-independent design is harder for a rival with purchase-linked schemes to copy without cannibalising its own programme (7 Powers counter-positioning); the pilot-to-scale timeline aims to build a lead in enrolled shops before a copy can match it.

risk_long: Members could resell tools or branded merchandise rather than using them, defeating the engagement purpose.
control_long: Items are chosen to have low resale value relative to their utility to the shop (branded, sized to the shop, consumable-dependent); audits flag members with high redemption but low subsequent referral activity.

risk_long: Shops could learn to recognise mystery riders and behave differently only during audits, biasing the measurement.
control_long: Audits are unannounced and run by a third-party agency with rotating personnel; the sample is drawn randomly each round from the full member list, not announced in advance; results are compared against the matched control districts, which the shops do not know are being tracked.

risk_long: If the retailer app is not live, has limited reach, or goes down, code logging has no reliable channel.
control_long: A22 reserves a one-time build or extension cost if no live app exists; a manual WhatsApp or SMS fallback for logging during outages; the pilot confirms the app's real capacity before scale.

risk_long: Costs per member, especially Tier 3 hardware, could run above the assumption register's bear case.
control_long: Spend is capped at the 1.5% to 2% envelope in every quarter (model check spend_within_envelope); member growth is phased (rollout table) so costs are visible before national scale; Tier 3 hardware can move to lease-only if the bear case breaches the cap.

risk_long: Without the annual brand-track re-survey, Eurogrip cannot confirm whether stocking and recommendation actually moved.
control_long: A32 reserves an annual budget line for the re-survey; G3 at the end of Q8 is explicitly gated on this re-run, making it a condition for calling the national phase complete.
